passage: In the polytechnic in a small town the group had a robot project due in ten days. Shalini had not turned up for the last three sessions or sent her drawings. Jatin caught Shalini at the bicycle stand after class, away from the others. "You seem off lately. Is something wrong, or is the work confusing?" Shalini looked down for a moment. "My father is in hospital in the city, and I go back on weekends. I did not want to say." Jatin nodded. "Then tell me which part is hard right now, and we will split the rest." Shalini breathed out. At the next meeting Ravi asked loudly why Shalini was missing, and Jatin said, "It is sorted."

qa.q: Where did Jatin speak to Shalini?
qa.a: Jatin caught Shalini at the bicycle stand after class, away from the others.

qa.q: What might Shalini have been feeling before telling Jatin about the hospital?
qa.a: Shalini was probably worried and tense, carrying a private worry about a family member and not wanting to say; the breath out shows relief when Jatin listened.

qa.q: What made Jatin's private question more helpful than raising it in the meeting?
qa.a: Jatin asked away from the others, without accusing, and offered to split the work, which let Shalini explain and kept the team from judging without knowing.

qa.q: Why might Ravi have asked loudly why Shalini was missing?
qa.a: Ravi may be annoyed at the extra work and unaware of the reason; without the private talk, absence looks like plain avoidance.

grounding: A team member asks a coasting member what is going on in private before escalating, and there is a hidden reason such as family illness.

passage: In a Manchester study group Mei had not touched the shared slides for two weeks. Kai and Priya were quietly furious. Dalia caught Mei at the vending machine. "Hey, no pressure, but what is going on? I noticed your part is empty." Mei shrugged and looked at the machine. "Honestly? I just have not felt like doing it. It seemed boring, and you all were doing fine." Dalia waited a moment. "Okay. It matters to me that the work is shared, so can you take the last slide by Thursday?" Mei sighed. "Fine." Dalia did not add a lecture. By Friday the slide was there, with a note: "Sorry, it was avoidance."

qa.q: How long had Mei not touched the shared slides?
qa.a: Mei had not touched the shared slides for two weeks.

qa.q: Why did Mei say "It seemed boring, and you all were doing fine"?
qa.a: Mei was avoiding the work and assuming others would cover it; the shrug shows little guilt at first, though the note later shows some.

qa.q: What did Dalia do that got the slide done without a fight?
qa.a: Dalia asked privately and calmly, said sharing mattered, and asked for one clear slide by Thursday without a lecture.

qa.q: What might Kai and Priya be feeling while Mei's part stays empty?
qa.a: Kai and Priya are probably angry and worried about the deadline, but quiet about it, letting resentment build without anyone speaking.

grounding: A team member asks a coasting member what is going on in private before escalating, and the reason turns out to be plain avoidance.

passage:
Seema had missed three group meetings for the economics project, and her section of the report was blank.
Farhan wanted to email the professor. “Let's just report her.”
“Give me one day,” Aparna said.
She found Seema in the college library, staring at a book she wasn't reading. Aparna sat beside her. “Hey. Is something going on? You've seemed far away.”
Seema's eyes filled. “My mother's in hospital. I'm going there every evening. I didn't want to use it as an excuse.”
Aparna nodded slowly. “Thank you for telling me. Let's swap. I'll write your section this week, you take the slides next week when things are calmer.”
Seema breathed out. Farhan, hearing later, said nothing about the professor again.

qa.q: Where did Aparna find Seema?
qa.a: In the college library, staring at a book she wasn't reading.

qa.q: How did Seema seem to feel when Aparna asked what was going on?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and ashamed, her eyes filling, worried her mother's illness would sound like an excuse.

qa.q: Why was talking privately first a wise choice?
qa.a: It uncovered a hidden reason, her mother's illness, so the team could adjust instead of punishing her.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt after hearing the reason?
qa.a: Farhan probably felt a bit embarrassed and more understanding, which is why Farhan dropped the idea of reporting her.

grounding: Shows a team member asking a coasting teammate privately what's happening before escalating, and discovering a hidden reason.

passage:
Hi Nirmala,
I hope you're okay. I'm writing just to you, not the group, because I'd rather ask than guess.
You haven't posted anything in our project folder for two weeks, and the others are starting to talk about telling Dr Menon. I didn't want that to happen without checking in with you first.
Is something going on? Sometimes the task list is confusing (honestly, I found the part about the survey sample confusing too). Or maybe something else is happening. Either way, you can tell me, and it stays between us.
If it's confusion, I'm happy to sit with you in the library on Thursday and go through it together.
Take care,
Ira

qa.q: How long has Nirmala not posted in the folder?
qa.a: For two weeks.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling while writing this email?
qa.a: Ira felt concerned and caring, worried about Nirmala and uneasy about the group going to Dr Menon without checking first.

qa.q: What makes Ira's email a good first step?
qa.a: It's private, doesn't accuse, offers possible reasons like confusion, and suggests a concrete way to help before anyone escalates.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel reading the email?
qa.a: Nirmala might feel relieved and less ashamed, especially seeing that Ira also found part of the task confusing.

grounding: A team member writes privately to a coasting teammate to ask what is going on before escalating, allowing for hidden confusion.

passage:
So you asked how we handled Indu in our final-year group? Right. I'm Chinmay.
Indu stopped doing her part in October. The others wanted to go straight to Professor Rao. I said, let me talk to her first. You never know. Last year a friend of mine was quietly ill and nobody knew.
I bought her coffee and asked, “What's going on? Anything I should know?”
She looked at her phone and said, “Nothing, just busy.” I asked if the task was confusing. She said, “Not really. I just don't feel like it.”
Honestly, that was clarifying. I told her kindly that we'd give her until Friday, and after that we'd talk to Professor Rao. She didn't do it, so we did. At least I knew I'd been fair.

qa.q: Who did the others want to go to?
qa.a: They wanted to go straight to Professor Rao.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel after Indu's honest answer?
qa.a: Chinmay felt clear and settled, even relieved, knowing it was plain avoidance and that the group had been fair.

qa.q: Why was it fair to talk to Indu before escalating?
qa.a: It gave her a chance to share a hidden reason like illness or confusion, and a clear deadline before going to the professor.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt when Chinmay asked what was going on?
qa.a: She may have felt a little awkward or guilty, looking at her phone, but also given a fair chance.

grounding: A student talks privately to a coasting teammate before escalating, and finds the reason is plain avoidance.

passage:
I'm Aarti, Vinita's lab partner, so I saw most of this from the next bench.
Our five-person team had a stats project due, and Pradeep hadn't done a thing in two weeks. Tanvi wanted to email the professor straight away. "He's just lazy," she said.
Vinita said, "Give me one day."
After class she caught Pradeep by the water cooler, away from us. I couldn't hear much, only that her voice stayed low and his shoulders slowly dropped. Later she told us, "He doesn't understand the software at all. He was too embarrassed to say, so he's been avoiding it." She'd offered to show him for an hour on Saturday. "And if nothing's done by Tuesday, we go to the professor together."
On Saturday I saw them in the library, two laptops open. By Tuesday Pradeep had uploaded his section. Not brilliant, but his.

qa.q: How long had Pradeep done nothing on the project?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What do Pradeep's slowly dropping shoulders suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Pradeep likely felt embarrassed at first and then relieved, as the problem he had been hiding finally came out in private.

qa.q: Why was talking to Pradeep privately first a good move?
qa.a: It uncovered the real reason, confusion plus avoidance, and gave him a fair chance and a clear deadline before going to the professor.

qa.q: How might Tanvi see Vinita's choice to wait one day?
qa.a: Tanvi may have felt impatient, sure Pradeep was simply lazy, but the result shows Tanvi there was more to it.

grounding: Shows a team member speaking privately to a coasting teammate before escalating, finding a hidden reason mixed with avoidance.
